o: Lord and Potter of my life, I come before you this morning with open hands. Thank you for giving me one more day, and thank you for not leaving me half-made. You began a work in me, and I know you are continuing it, even when I sometimes resist and harden like a dried-out vessel.

Today I want to tell you sincerely: make of me what you will. I have my plans, my desires and my projects, but I recognize that you see what I cannot see. If something doesn't go the way I hoped, help me believe that you are not absent and that all things work together for good for those who love you. Take away my pride, my impatience and my habit of wanting to control everything. Shape my character with love.

Give me a teachable heart to accept your direction. May every encounter today be a chance to reflect your goodness, and every setback a lesson in your hands. Take care of my family, my work and my decisions. When I feel tired, remind me that clay does not grow weary in the potter's hands. And when I have to wait, teach me to rest in the fact that your timing is perfect. Thank you, because you are not finished with me. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: On this day, November 27, 1862, Adelaide Addison Pollard was born in Bloomfield, Iowa. She would become a Bible teacher and the author of more than a hundred hymns and gospel songs. She studied in several places, taught in girls' schools, and later devoted herself to teaching the Scriptures from town to town.

From her youth she felt a desire to serve as a missionary in Africa. Around 1902 she worked to gather the necessary resources, but the money never came and the door did not open. It was a great disappointment. With a heavy heart, she attended a prayer meeting. There, an elderly woman asked the Lord to have His way in the lives of everyone present.

That simple prayer stayed in Adelaide's heart. When she got home, she meditated on the passage in Jeremiah about the potter working the clay on his wheel. The vessel was spoiled in his hands, and he made it again into another vessel, as it seemed good to him. From that meditation sprang the words of a hymn we still know today: Have Thine Own Way, Lord, sung as a prayer of surrender to the Lord.

Years later, Adelaide taught at a missionary training school in Nyack, New York, and was able to go to Africa for a brief period before World War I. She died on December 20, 1934. Her life shows that a closed door does not mean a lost purpose. Sometimes God uses our disappointment to give the world a song of surrender.
m.c: Walk through this day with the peace of one who knows he is in good hands. What the Lord has begun in you, He will carry on to completion. Be courageous, be patient, and receive His grace with every step you take today.
m: There are days when our plans run into a closed door. Adelaide Pollard experienced it with her desire to go to Africa, and her story reminds us that disappointment is not the end. When she surrendered her disillusionment to God, a hymn was born that has accompanied believers for many generations.

Paul uses the image of the potter in his letter to the Romans. He asks: will the thing formed say to the one who formed it, “Why have you made me like this?” The potter has rights over the clay. This is not a statement meant to frighten us, but to reassure us. The One who made us knows the design, knows how long the work takes, and does not make mistakes in the process.

In the same letter there is a promise that sustains those who wait: for those who love God, all things work together for their good. It does not say that all things are good, but that God directs them toward good. That includes disappointed plans, long waits, and letdowns we do not understand. Nothing remains outside His watchful hand.

For today, I suggest a concrete prayer of surrender. Think of something you have insisted on in your own way, and tell God about it frankly: Lord, let your will be done here. Then, as you go about your tasks, act with gentleness and attention to what God will place before you. Perhaps a conversation, a humble task, or a change of route. Whoever lets himself be shaped discovers that God did have a purpose.

o: Lord Jesus, as I close this day, I thank you for being with me every moment. Thank you for the strength to work, for the people who helped me, and for the opportunities to serve that you placed in my path. Thank you also for the times you corrected me tenderly, because that is how you help me grow.

Today I think of you, who, being Lord and Master, rose from the table, wrapped a towel around your waist and washed your disciples' feet. What a great example of love without pride. Forgive me for the times I wanted to be served instead of serving, or when I let a kind gesture pass because I felt tired. Teach me to see the small needs that others do not notice.

I place in your hands the burdens of this day: the rushing, the poorly chosen words, the unfinished tasks. May your peace take the place of my worries. Bless my family as they rest and watch over those who feel lonely today. Renew my body and spirit during the night, and wake me with a heart ready to serve. Thank you, because your love is faithful and your grace reaches me every day. In Jesus' name, amen.
h: The night before His crucifixion, Jesus gathered with His disciples for the meal. The Gospel of John says that He knew the Father had put all things into His hands, and that He had come from God and was going back to God. With that full awareness of who He was, He did something no one expected.

He rose from the table, took off His outer garments, picked up a towel and wrapped it around Himself. Then He poured water into a basin and began to wash His disciples' feet, drying them with the towel. In that day, this was the work of the lowest-ranking servant, since the roads were dusty and sandals left feet dirty. None of the twelve had offered to do it.

When it came to Peter's turn, he resisted. He could not accept that his Master would do something so humble for him. Jesus explained that what He was doing, Peter would not understand now, but would understand later. What Peter learned that night is that Christ's love stoops to the lowest place to cleanse and restore.

When He had finished, Jesus returned to the table and asked them if they understood what He had done. He told them that if He, being Lord and Master, had washed their feet, they ought also to wash one another's feet. He had given them an example, so that they would do as He had done. Ever since, Christians have remembered that true leadership looks more like a towel than a crown.
t.c: Now lay down everything that weighed on your day, and let the Lord's peace rest on your home. Whoever serves with love never works in vain. May your sleep be deep, your heart calm, and your morning a fresh sign of His grace.
m: When the day ends, we are used to asking ourselves what we accomplished. Jesus also invites us to ask whom we served. The scene of the foot washing is one of the most moving in the Gospel, because it shows the greatness of God clothed in simplicity. The One who had everything in His hands knelt down to care for the tired feet of His friends.

This story dismantles our idea of importance. We often believe we have value because of what we command, what we earn, or who recognizes us. Jesus teaches the opposite: let whoever wants to be great serve. He did not only say it in words, but with a towel and a basin of water. Serving does not take away our dignity; it makes us like Him.

Notice that Jesus washed even the feet of the one who would betray Him and the one who would deny Him. His service did not depend on the merits of others. This challenges us to serve even those we don't like, those who don't thank us, or those who have hurt us. It is not easy, but it is possible when we remember how much we have received.

Before sleeping, I suggest a brief exercise. Remember a moment today when you could have served and did not, and ask forgiveness without dramatizing it. Then think of one concrete action for tomorrow: preparing something for someone, listening without interrupting, helping quietly. Give it all to the Lord and sleep peacefully. Humble service is a form of worship that God receives with pleasure.
